Novel PFAS destruction technologies under investigation include electrochemical oxidation ( Carter and Farrell, 2008 ; Rusinek, 2019 ), sonochemical destruction ( Cheng et al., 2008 ), high-temperature incineration ( US EPA, 2020 ), alkaline hydrolysis ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Hao et al., 2021 ), plasma treatment ( Stratton et al., 2017 ; Singh et al., 2019 ), and others ( Kucharzyk et al., 2017 ; Dombrowski et al., 2018 ). While most of the aforementioned technologies have been demonstrated to destroy PFOS and PFOA, few have demonstrated the ability to destroy the entire class of PFAS molecules, and several are known to produce short-chain PFAS as treatment byproducts. Thus far, alkaline hydrolysis ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Hao et al., 2021 ) appears to show the most promise for effective and complete destruction of all PFAS. The high pressures of the contained hydrothermal reaction environment are partially responsible for the success of the alkaline hydrolysis process, as low molecular weight (MW) species remain con - tained and react to completion.

Most existing PFAS degradation studies focus on environmentally relevant trace levels (ng/L to µ g/L) typically found in surface water and groundwater. In contrast, this study addresses higher PFAS concentrations representative of concentrated waste streams, such as concentrates of membrane filtration or regener - ation solutions from adsorption processes (e.g. electrosorption), aqueous film-forming foams (AFFF), industrial discharges, and landfill leachate. Furthermore, quantification of fluoride release which is relevant for degradation verification requires working in the mg/L PFAS concen - tration range as trace fluoride quantification is difficult. In this work, the experimental investigation was carried out using an orifice-type HC system to evaluate PFAS degradation and defluorination in a tap water matrix. The HC process offers a chemical-, catalyst- and waste-free treatment strategy. Leveraging the extreme physical and chemical conditions created during cavitation events, our approach specifically targets long-chain PFAS such as PFOS, one of the most persistent and recalcitrant compounds within the PFAS family. Treat - ment variables included reaction time, number of passes through the HC reactor, and initial PFOS concentration, all under a constant inlet pres - sure of 48 bar. Fluoride ion release was used as a primary indicator of C – F bond cleavage, providing quantitative insight into degradation ef - ficiency.

It presents a viable alternative to conventional treatment methods and lays the groundwork for sustainable, large-scale PFAS remediation strategies. Further efforts in optimizing HC reactor geometry and operating conditions are essential to enhance PFAS breakdown and defluorination efficiency, enabling successful upscaling and imple - mentation at diverse sites such as AFFF, industrial facilities and WWTPs. Here, we present a case study of AFFF destruction in a batch HALT reactor to demonstrate the process efficacy and to demon- strate the performance of a recently discovered proprietary catalytic material. The performance of the proprietary catalyst indicates that the HALT process could be optimized at the industrial scale to in- crease reaction rates, decreasing the necessary reaction residence time and, correspondingly, the necessary reactor size.
